Help yourself - it's CC0 which means you can use this pic however you like without asking permission including selling it :) Stunning crab apple tree (one of two close together at what3words.com/wiped.mirror.talent) in Greenwich Park. I'm tagging this as cherry blossom even though it's technically not because it's pink, gorgeous, blossomy and photogenic. I don't know anything about crab apples but it might be a Malus Royalty or a Malus Rudolph. I think cherry trees are Prunus something or other. The tree(s) in this photo blossom earlier than the Greenwich Cherry Tree vista near Rangers House, which should be blossoming within the next week or so.

Categories.value: NGC 6744|Flickr images reviewed by FlickreviewR|Hubble images of galaxies|Photos in Flickr Explore|Featured pictures of galaxies

ImageDescription.value:
Well-known for its similarity to the Milky Way, looking at NGC 6744 is kind of like looking into a cosmic mirror. We will almost certainly never know what our own galaxy looks like from afar, but we can look across the void and try to find something very similar.

Just like we see here, The Milky Way is known to have a central bar full of older, yellower stars, and a bulge. Some say the bulge is peanut-shaped, but I am sure it's more of an X, though I can see how it could also be described as a peanut. I have noted the X feature in the cores of a few other galaxies, and while it seems to be a fairly common morphology, I think it's only visible when viewed edge-on, so we can't see it here.

Moving out from the core, dusty lanes and pink nebulas of star-formation are also evident. When given a wider field of view, two arms a little more than vaguely defined can be seen. Numerous spurs and disconnects give it a halfway chaotic or fluffy, flocculent appearance.

I was gathering a few resources and references here and there to attempt an illustration of the Milky Way and Andromeda paired together from some distant vantage point when I discovered this galaxy was indeed in the Hubble archive. Not only that, but it's got a fantastic set of filters to work with and is part of the wonderful Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey (LEGUS) which is chock full of intimate views of a variety of galaxies.

This image is possible thanks to the following two proposals:

LEGUS: Legacy ExtraGalactic UV Survey - HST Proposal 13364

H-alpha LEGUS: Unveiling the Interplay Between Stars, Star Clusters, and Ionized Gas - HST Proposal 13773

Note: Data for this image can be downloaded from the HLA, but the processing is better if you download it from this page: archive.stsci.edu/prepds/legus/dataproducts-public.html

The F657N data is not on the LEGUS page and must be obtained from the HLA as of this writing.

Red: WFC3/UVIS F657N + WFC3/UVIS F814W Green: WFC3/UVIS F555W Blue: WFC3/UVIS F275W + WFC3/UVIS F336W + WFC3/UVIS F438W

North is 148.8° clockwise from up.

Artist.value: Judy Schmidt from USA

157222106.title: File:Rainbow walkway AROS art museum Aarhus Denmark 14.jpg

ObjectName.value: Rainbow walkway AROS art museum Aarhus Denmark 14

Categories.value: Self-published work|Orange and pink|Curved structures|Interior of Your Rainbow Panorama|Windows in Aarhus|March in Aarhus

ImageDescription.value: Standing inside Olafur Eliasson’s installation ‘Your rainbow panorama’: a 150-metre long, three-metre-wide circular walkway in glass in all the colours of the spectrum. It's 50 metres above the city of Aarhus, Denmark - a permanent art installation on top of ARoS Kunstmuseum. (Aarhus International Art Museum). There are 360° views over the city. The colours and light and mood change as you walk and according to the weather and time of day. We are standing in the section with vivid primary shades of pink and purple and orange. The walkway ahead of us is empty. Through the two curving sweeps of glass enclosing us, we see the city spread out for several kilometres below a sky dotted with white fluffy clouds. We can clearly see that we are looking East across Aarhus. We can see the harbour and sea and the woodland promontory. We can see roads, streets, traffic lights, and mid-city and harbourside buildings including Aarhus Domkirke (cathedral); the historic courthouse; giant landmark harbour cranes. Everything we see is clear, but coloured in a jumble of tones of reds and oranges and pinks. It is an almost disorientating effect - the shape of the city and everything in it is correct and familiar, but at the same time, everything is so vividly orange and pink that it looks strange, like a civic doppelganger.
